entries.bbb3c617e2ea0b89060e48e6c8677bce0ec92a55: <div sID="gen3055" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Num.19" sID="Num.19"/> <div eID="gen3055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3056" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3057" type="x-p"/> This chapter is only concerning the preparing and using of the ashes which were to impregnate the water of purification. The people had complained of the strictness of the law, which forbade their near approach to the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Num.17.13">ch. xvii. 13</reference>. In answer to this complaint, they are here directed to purify themselves, so as that they might come as far as they had occasion without fear. Here is, I. The method of preparing these ashes, by the burning of a red heifer, with a great deal of ceremony, <reference osisRef="Num.19.1-Num.19.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. The way of using them. 1. They were designed to purify persons from the pollution contracted by a dead body, <reference osisRef="Num.19.11-Num.19.16">ver. 11-16</reference>. 2. They were to be put into running water (a small quantity of them), with which the person to be cleansed must be purified, <reference osisRef="Num.19.17-Num.19.22">ver. 17-22</reference>. And that this ceremonial purification was a type and figure of the cleansing of the consciences of believers from the pollutions of sin appears by the apostle's discourse, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13-Heb.9.14">Heb. ix. 13, 14</reference>, where he compares the efficacy of the blood of Christ with the sanctifying virtue that was in "the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean."
entries.bbfe8b43ac38d9045a5c8b024300ac527a967b91: <div eID="gen3057" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3056" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Ashes of Purification. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1471.)</title> <div sID="gen3058" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses and unto Aaron, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the ordinance of the law which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath commanded, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring thee a red heifer without spot, wherein <hi type="italic">is</hi> no blemish, <hi type="italic">and</hi> upon which never came yoke: <hi type="super">3</hi> And ye shall give her unto Eleazar the priest, that he may bring her forth without the camp, and <hi type="italic">one</hi> shall slay her before his face: <hi type="super">4</hi> And Eleazar the priest shall take of her blood with his finger, and sprinkle of her blood directly before the tabernacle of the congregation seven times: <hi type="super">5</hi> And <hi type="italic">one</hi> shall burn the heifer in his sight; her skin, and her flesh, and her blood, with her dung, shall he burn: <hi type="super">6</hi> And the priest shall take cedar wood, and hyssop, and scarlet, and cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the midst of the burning of the heifer. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then the priest shall wash his clothes, and he shall bathe his flesh in water, and afterward he shall come into the camp, and the priest shall be unclean until the even. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he that burneth her shall wash his clothes in water, and bathe his flesh in water, and shall be unclean until the even. <hi type="super">9</hi> And a man <hi type="italic">that is</hi> clean shall gather up the ashes of the heifer, and lay <hi type="italic">them</hi> up without the camp in a clean place, and it shall be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel for a water of separation: it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a purification for sin. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he that gathereth the ashes of the heifer shall wash his clothes, and be unclean until the even: and it shall be unto the children of Israel, and unto the stranger that sojourneth among them, for a statute for ever. <div eID="gen3058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3059" type="x-p"/> We have here the divine appointment concerning the solemn burning of a red heifer to ashes, and the preserving of the ashes, that of them might be made, not a beautifying, but a purifying, water, for that was the utmost the law reached to; it offered not to adorn as the gospel does, but to cleanse only. This burning of the heifer, though it was not properly a sacrifice of expiation, being not performed at the altar, yet was typical of the death and sufferings of Christ, by which he intended, not only to satisfy God's justice, but to purify and pacify our consciences, that we may have peace with God and also peace in our own bosoms, to prepare for which Christ died, not only like the bulls and goats at the altar, but like the heifer without the camp. <div eID="gen3059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3060" type="x-p"/> I. There was a great deal of care employed in the choice of the heifer that was to be burnt, much more than in the choice of any other offering, <reference osisRef="Num.19.2">v. 2</reference>. It must not only be without blemish, typifying the spotless purity and sinless perfection of the Lord Jesus, but it must a red heifer, because of the rarity of the colour, that it might be the more remarkable: the Jews say, "If but two hairs were black or white, it was unlawful." Christ, as man, was the Son of Adam, <hi type="italic">red earth,</hi> and we find him red in his apparel, red with his own blood, and red with the blood of his enemies. And it must be one on which never came yoke, which was not insisted on in other sacrifices, but thus was typified the voluntary offer of the Lord Jesus, when he said, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come,</hi> He was bound and held with no other cords than those of his own love. This heifer was to be provided at the expense of the congregation, because they were all to have a joint interest in it; and so all believers have in Christ. <div eID="gen3060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3061" type="x-p"/> II. There was to be a great deal of ceremony in the burning of it. The care of doing it was committed to Eleazar, not to Aaron himself, because it was not fit that he should do any thing to render himself ceremonially unclean, no, not so much as <hi type="italic">till the evening</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.19.8">v. 8</reference>); yet it being an affair of great concern especially in the significancy of it, it was to be performed by him that was next to Aaron in dignity. The chief priests of that time had the principal hand in the death of Christ. Now, <div eID="gen3061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3062" type="x-p"/> 1. The heifer was to be slain without the camp, as an impure thing, which bespeaks the insufficiency of the methods prescribed by the ceremonial law to take away sin. So far were they from cleansing effectually that they were themselves unclean; as if the pollution that was laid upon them continued to cleave to them. Yet, to answer this type, our Lord Jesus, being made sin and a curse for us, <hi type="italic">suffered without the gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.12">Heb. xiii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen3062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3063" type="x-p"/> 2. Eleazar was to <hi type="italic">sprinkle the blood directly before the door of the tabernacle,</hi> and looking steadfastly towards it, <reference osisRef="Num.19.4">v. 4</reference>. This made it in some sort an expiation; for the sprinkling of the blood before the Lord was the chief solemnity in all the sacrifices of atonement; therefore, though this was not done at the altar, yet, being done towards the sanctuary, it was intimated that the virtue and validity of it depended upon the sanctuary, and were derived from it. This signified the satisfaction that was made to God by the death of Christ, our great high priest, who <hi type="italic">by the eternal Spirit</hi> (and the Spirit is called the finger of God, as Ainsworth observes, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.20">Luke xi. 20</reference>) <hi type="italic">offered himself without spot unto God;</hi> directly before the sanctuary, when he said, <hi type="italic">Father, into thy hands I commit my spirit.</hi> It also signifies how necessary it was to the purifying of our hearts that satisfaction should be made to divine justice. This sprinkling of the blood put virtue into the ashes. <div eID="gen3063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3064" type="x-p"/> 3. The heifer was to be <hi type="italic">wholly burnt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.19.5">v. 5</reference>. This typified the extreme sufferings of our Lord Jesus, both in soul and body, as a sacrifice made by fire. The priest was to cast into the fire, while it was burning, cedarwood, hyssop, and scarlet, which were used in the cleansing of lepers (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.6-Lev.14.7">Lev. xiv. 6, 7</reference>), that the ashes of these might be mingled with the ashes of the heifer, because they were designed for purification. <div eID="gen3064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3065" type="x-p"/> 4. The ashes of the heifer (separated as well as they could from the ashes of the wood wherewith it was burnt) were to be carefully gathered up by the hand of a clean person, and (as the Jews say) pounded and sifted, and so laid up for the use of the congregation, as there was occasion (<reference osisRef="Num.19.9">v. 9</reference>), not only for that generation, but for posterity; for the ashes of this one heifer were sufficient to season as many vessels of water as the people of Israel would need for many ages. The Jews say that this one served till the captivity, nearly 1000 years, and that there was never another heifer burnt till Ezra's time, after their return, to which tradition of theirs, grounded (I suppose) only upon the silence of their old records, I see no reason we have to give credit, since in the later times of their church, of which they had more full records, they find eight burnt between Ezra's time and the destruction of the second temple, which was about 500 years, These ashes are said to be laid up here as <hi type="italic">a purification for sin,</hi> because, though they were intended to purify only from ceremonial uncleanness, yet they were a type of that purification for sin which our Lord Jesus made by his death. Ashes mixed with water are used in scouring, but these had their virtue purely from the divine institution, and their accomplishment and perfection in Christ, who is <hi type="italic">the end of this law for righteousness.</hi> Now observe, (1.) That the water of purification was made so by the ashes of a heifer, whose blood was sprinkled before the sanctuary; so that which cleanses our consciences is the abiding virtue of the death of Christ; it is his blood that <hi type="italic">cleanses from all sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.1.7">1 John i. 7</reference>. (2.) That the ashes were sufficient for all the people. There needed not to be a fresh heifer slain for every person or family that had occasion to be purified, but this one was enough for all, even for the strangers that sojourned among them (<reference osisRef="Num.19.10">v. 10</reference>); so there is virtue enough in the blood of Christ for all that repent and believe the gospel, for every Israelite, and not for their sins only, but for <hi type="italic">the sins of the whole world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.2">1 John ii. 2</reference>. (3.) That these ashes were capable of being preserved without waste to many ages. No bodily substance is so incorruptible as ashes are, which (says bishop Patrick) made these a very fit emblem of the everlasting efficacy of the sacrifice of Christ. He is able to save, and, in order to that, able to cleanse, to the uttermost, both of person and times. (4.) These ashes were laid up as a stock or treasure, for the constant purification of Israel from their pollutions; so the blood of Christ is laid up for us in the word and sacraments, as an inexhaustible fountain of merit, to which by faith we may have recourse daily for the purging of our consciences; see <reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zech. xiii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen3065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3066" type="x-p"/> 5. All those that were employed in this service were made ceremonially unclean by it; even Eleazar himself, though he did but sprinkle the blood, <reference osisRef="Num.19.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">He that burned the heifer was unclean</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.19.8">v. 8</reference>), and he that <hi type="italic">gathered up the ashes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.19.10">v. 10</reference>); so all that had a hand in putting Christ to death contracted guilt by it: his betrayer, his prosecutors, his judge, his executioner, all did what they did with wicked hands, though it was <hi type="italic">by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>); yet some of them were, and all might have been cleansed by the virtue of that same blood which they had brought themselves under the guilt of. Some make this to signify the imperfection of the legal services, and their insufficiency to take away sin, inasmuch as those who prepared for the purifying of others were themselves polluted by the preparation. The Jews say, This is a mystery which Solomon himself did not understand, that the same thing should pollute those that were clean and purify those that were unclean. But (says bishop Patrick) it is not strange to those who consider that all the sacrifices which were offered for sin were therefore looked upon as impure, because the sins of men were laid upon them, as all our sins were upon Christ, who therefore is said to be <hi type="italic">made sin for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2 Cor. v. 21</reference>.
entries.c952af8f3582d7af95ca515752e02e22639c3c98: <div eID="gen3066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3067" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. <hi type="super">12</hi> He shall purify himself with it on the third day, and on the seventh day he shall be clean: but if he purify not himself the third day, then the seventh day he shall not be clean. <hi type="super">13</hi> Whosoever toucheth the dead body of any man that is dead, and purifieth not himself, defileth the tabernacle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and that soul shall be cut off from Israel: because the water of separation was not sprinkled upon him, he shall be unclean; his uncleanness <hi type="italic">is</hi> yet upon him. <hi type="super">14</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law, when a man dieth in a tent: all that come into the tent, and all that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the tent, shall be unclean seven days. <hi type="super">15</hi> And every open vessel, which hath no covering bound upon it, <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean. <hi type="super">16</hi> And whosoever toucheth one that is slain with a sword in the open fields, or a dead body, or a bone of a man, or a grave, shall be unclean seven days. <hi type="super">17</hi> And for an unclean <hi type="italic">person</hi> they shall take of the ashes of the burnt heifer of purification for sin, and running water shall be put thereto in a vessel: <hi type="super">18</hi> And a clean person shall take hyssop, and dip <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the water, and sprinkle <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon the tent, and upon all the vessels, and upon the persons that were there, and upon him that touched a bone, or one slain, or one dead, or a grave: <hi type="super">19</hi> And the clean <hi type="italic">person</hi> shall sprinkle upon the unclean on the third day, and on the seventh day: and on the seventh day he shall purify himself, and wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and shall be clean at even. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the man that shall be unclean, and shall not purify himself, that soul shall be cut off from among the congregation, because he hath defiled the sanctuary of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : the water of separation hath not been sprinkled upon him; he <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean. <hi type="super">21</hi> And it shall be a perpetual statute unto them, that he that sprinkleth the water of separation shall wash his clothes; and he that toucheth the water of separation shall be unclean until even. <hi type="super">22</hi> And whatsoever the unclean <hi type="italic">person</hi> toucheth shall be unclean; and the soul that toucheth <hi type="italic">it</hi> shall be unclean until even. <div eID="gen3067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3068" type="x-p"/> Directions are here given concerning the use and application of the ashes which were prepared for purification. they were laid up to be laid out; and therefore, though now one place would serve to keep them in, while all Israel lay so closely encamped, yet it is probable that afterwards, when they came to Canaan, some of these ashes were kept in every town, for there would be daily use for them. Observe, <div eID="gen3068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3069" type="x-p"/> I. In what cases there needed a purification with these ashes. No other is mentioned here than the ceremonial uncleanness that was contracted by the touch of a dead body, or of the bone or grave of a dead man, or being in the tent or house where a dead body lay, <reference osisRef="Num.19.11">v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.19.14-Num.19.16">14-16</reference>. This I look upon to have been one of the greatest burdens of the ceremonial law, and one of the most unaccountable. He that touched the carcase of an unclean beast, or any living man under the greatest ceremonial uncleanness, was made unclean by it only <hi type="italic">till the evening,</hi> and needed only common water to purify himself with; but he that came near the dead body of man, woman, or child, much bear the reproach of his uncleanness seven days, must twice be purified with the water of separation, which he could not obtain without trouble and charge, and till he was purified must not come near the sanctuary upon pain of death. <div eID="gen3069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3070" type="x-p"/> 1. This was strange, considering, (1.) that whenever any died (and we are in deaths oft) several persons must unavoidable contract this pollution, the body must be stripped, washed, wound up, carried out, and buried, and this could not be done without many hands, and yet all defiled, which signifies that in our corrupt and fallen state there is none that lives and sins not; we cannot avoid being polluted by the defiling world we pass through, and we offend daily, yet the impossibility of our being sinless does not make sin the less polluting. (2.) that taking care of the dead, to see them decently buried, is not only necessary, but a very good office, and an act of kindness, both to the honour of the dead and the comfort of the living, and yet uncleanness was contracted by it, which intimates that the pollutions of sin mix with and cleave to our best services. <hi type="italic">There is not a just man upon earth that doeth good and sinneth not;</hi> we are apt some way or other to do amiss even in our doing good. (3.) That this pollution was contracted by what was done privately in their own houses, which intimates (as bishop Patrick observes) that God sees what is done in secret, and nothing can be concealed from the divine Majesty. (4.) This pollution might be contracted, and yet a man might never know it, as by the touch of a grave which appeared not, of which our Saviour says, Those that <hi type="italic">walk over it are not aware of it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.44">Luke xi. 44</reference>), which intimates the defilement of the conscience by sins of ignorance, and the cause we have to cry out, "Who can understand his errors?" and to pray, "Cleanse us from secret faults, faults which we ourselves do not see ourselves guilty of." <div eID="gen3070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3071" type="x-p"/> 2. But why did the law make a dead corpse such a defiling thing? (1.) Because death is the <hi type="italic">wages of sin, entered into the world</hi> by it, and reigns by the power of it. Death to mankind is another thing from what it is to other creatures: it is a curse, it is the execution of the law, and therefore the defilement of death signifies the defilement of sin. (2.) Because the law could not conquer death, nor abolish it and alter the property of it, as the gospel does by bringing life and immortality to light, and so introducing a better hope. Since our Redeemer was dead and buried, death is no more destroying to the Israel of God, and therefore dead bodies are no more defiling; but while the church was under the law, to show that it <hi type="italic">made not the comers thereunto perfect,</hi> the pollution contracted by dead bodies could not but form in their minds melancholy and uncomfortable notions concerning death, while believers now through Christ can triumph over it. <hi type="italic">O grave! where is thy victory?</hi> Where is thy pollution? <div eID="gen3071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3072" type="x-p"/> II. How the ashes were to be used and applied in these cases. 1. A small quantity of the ashes must be put into a cup of spring water, and mixed with the water, which thereby was made, as it is here called, a <hi type="italic">water of separation,</hi> because it was to be sprinkled on those who were separated or removed from the sanctuary by their uncleanness. As the ashes of the heifer signified the merit of Christ, so the running water signified the power and grace of the blessed Spirit, who is compared to rivers of living water; and it is by his operation that the righteousness of Christ is applied to us for our cleansing. Hence we are said to be washed, that is, sanctified and justified, not only in the name of the Lord Jesus, but by the <hi type="italic">Spirit of our God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. vi. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1 Pet. i. 2</reference>. Those that promise themselves benefit by the righteousness of Christ, while they submit not to the grace and influence of the Spirit, do but deceive themselves, for we cannot put asunder what God has joined, nor be purified by the ashes otherwise than in the running water. 2. This water must be applied by a bunch of hyssop dipped in it, with which the person or thing to be cleansed must be sprinkled (<reference osisRef="Num.19.18">v. 18</reference>), in allusion to which David prays, <hi type="italic">Purge me with hyssop.</hi> Faith is the bunch of hyssop wherewith the conscience is sprinkled and the heart purified. Many might be sprinkled at once, and the water with which the ashes were mingled might serve for many sprinklings, till it was all spent; and a very little lighting upon a man served to purify him, if done with that intention. In allusion to this application of the water of separation by sprinkling, the blood of Christ is said to be the <hi type="italic">blood of sprinkling</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.24">Heb. xii. 24</reference>), and with it were are said to be <hi type="italic">sprinkled from an evil conscience</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">Heb. x. 22</reference>), that is, we are freed from the uneasiness that arises from a sense of our guilt. And it is foretold that Christ, by his baptism, shall <hi type="italic">sprinkle many nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.52.15">Isa. lii. 15</reference>. 3. The unclean person must be sprinkled with this water on <hi type="italic">the third day</hi> after his pollution, and <hi type="italic">on the seventh day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.19.12-Num.19.19">v. 12-19</reference>. The days were reckoned (we may suppose) from the last time of his touching or coming near the dead body; for he would not begin the days of his cleansing while he was still under a necessity of repeating the pollution; but when the dead body was buried, so that there was no further occasion of meddling with it, then he began to reckon his days. Then, and then only, we may with comfort apply Christ's merit to our souls, when we have forsaken sin, and cease all <hi type="italic">fellowship with the unfruitful works of</hi> death and <hi type="italic">darkness.</hi> The repetition of the sprinkling teaches us often to renew the actings of repentance and faith, wash as Naaman, <hi type="italic">seven times;</hi> we need to do that often which is so necessary to be well done. 4. Though the pollution contracted was only ceremonial, yet the neglect of the purification prescribed would turn into moral guilt: <hi type="italic">He that shall be unclean</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">not purify himself, that soul shall be cut off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.19.20">v. 20</reference>. Note, It is a dangerous thing to contemn divine institutions, though they may seem minute. A slight wound, if neglected, may prove fatal; a sin we call little, if not repented of, will be our ruin, when great sinners that repent shall find mercy. Our uncleanness separates us from God, but it is our being unclean and not purifying ourselves that will separate us for ever from him: it is not the wound that is fatal, so much as the contempt of the remedy. 5. Even he that <hi type="italic">sprinkled the water of separation,</hi> or <hi type="italic">touched</hi> it, or <hi type="italic">touched the unclean person,</hi> must be <hi type="italic">unclean till the evening,</hi> that is, must not come near the sanctuary on that day, <reference osisRef="Num.19.21-Num.19.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. Thus God would show them the imperfection of those services, and their insufficiency to purify the conscience, that they might look for the Messiah, who in the fulness of time should by the eternal Spirit offer himself without spot unto God, and so <hi type="italic">purge our consciences from dead works</hi> (that is, from sin, which defiles like a dead body, and is therefore called a <hi type="italic">body of death</hi>), that we may have liberty of access to the sanctuary, to serve the living God with living sacrifices.  <chapter eID="Num.19"/> <div eID="gen3072" type="x-p"/>

entries.1ee04779549e9bf04c657cfe022c765c19dc74a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1441"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.19.1-Num.19.22">Nu 19:1-22</reference>. The Water of Separation.</title> <div sID="gen1938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1441"/><hi type="bold">2. This is the ordinance of the law--</hi>an institution of a peculiar nature ordained by law for the purification of sin, and provided at the public expense because it was for the good of the whole community.<div eID="gen1938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring thee a red heifer without spot, &c.--</hi>This is the only case in which the color of the victim is specified. It has been supposed the ordinance was designed in opposition to the superstitious notions of the Egyptians. That people never offered a vow but they sacrificed a red bull, the greatest care being taken by their priests in examining whether it possessed the requisite characteristics, and it was an annual offering to Typhon, their evil being. By the choice, both of the sex and the color, provision was made for eradicating from the minds of the Israelites a favorite Egyptian superstition regarding two objects of their animal worship. <div eID="gen1939" type="x-p"/>
entries.626f79fc6fb16e661f2981928452787bbfcc64bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1442"/><div sID="gen1940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1442"/><hi type="bold">3-6. ye shall give her unto Eleazar the priest that he may bring her forth without the camp--</hi>He was the second or deputy high priest, and he was selected for this duty because the execution of it entailed temporary defilement, from which the acting high priest was to be preserved with the greatest care. It was led "forth without the camp," in accordance with the law regarding victims laden with the sins of the people, and thus typical of Christ (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.12">He 13:12</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Lev.24.14">Le 24:14</reference>). The priest was to sprinkle the blood "seven times" before--literally, "towards" or "near" the tabernacle, a description which seems to imply either that he carried a portion of the blood in a basin to the door of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.17">Le 4:17</reference>), or that in the act of sprinkling he turned his face towards the sacred edifice, being disqualified through the defiling influence of this operation from approaching close to it. By this attitude he indicated that he was presenting an expiatory sacrifice, for the acceptance of which he hoped, in the grace of God, by looking to the mercy seat. Every part of it was consumed by fire except the blood used in sprinkling, and the ingredients mixed with the ashes were the same as those employed in the sprinkling of lepers (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.4-Lev.14.7">Le 14:4-7</reference>). It was a water of separation--that is, of "sanctification" for the people of Israel. <div eID="gen1940" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae958f95967a3bc9eebeaae2c19953f35e06fd19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1443"/><div sID="gen1941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1443"/><hi type="bold">7. the priest shall be unclean until the even--</hi>The ceremonies prescribed show the imperfection of the Levitical priesthood, while they typify the condition of Christ when expiating our sins (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>). <div eID="gen1941" type="x-p"/>
entries.83183868404cc42e6926991ec1a77f51f5227a5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1444"/><div sID="gen1942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1444"/><hi type="bold">11-22. He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean--</hi>This law is noticed here to show the uses to which the water of separation [Nu 19:9] was applied. The case of a death is one; and as in every family which sustained a bereavement the members of the household became defiled, so in an immense population, where instances of mortality and other cases of uncleanness would be daily occurring, the water of separation must have been in constant requisition. To afford the necessary supply of the cleansing mixture, the Jewish writers say that a red heifer was sacrificed every year, and that the ashes, mingled with the sprinkling ingredients, were distributed through all the cities and towns of Israel. <div eID="gen1942" type="x-p"/>

entries.54ed21b3a1033dc881185be6ec8ce95ca9c8b9a0: <div eID="gen5738" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5739" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5740" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5740" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5739" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5741" type="x-p"/> The ordinance of the red heifer, <reference osisRef="Num.19.1">Num 19:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.19.2">Num 19:2</reference>. She shall be slain by Eleazar without the camp, and her blood sprinkled before the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Num.19.3">Num 19:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.19.4">Num 19:4</reference>. Her whole body and appurtenance shall be reduced to ashes, and while burning, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop, shall be thrown into the fire, <reference osisRef="Num.19.5">Num 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.19.6">Num 19:6</reference>. The priest, and he that burns her, to bathe themselves, and be reputed unclean till the evening, <reference osisRef="Num.19.7">Num 19:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.19.8">Num 19:8</reference>. Her ashes to be laid up for a water of purification, <reference osisRef="Num.19.9">Num 19:9</reference>. How, and in what cases it is to be applied, <reference osisRef="Num.19.10-Num.19.13">Num 19:10-13</reference>. The law concerning him who dies in a tent, or who is killed in the open field, <reference osisRef="Num.19.14-Num.19.16">Num 19:14-16</reference>. How the persons, tent, and vessels are to be purified by the application of these ashes, <reference osisRef="Num.19.17-Num.19.19">Num 19:17-19</reference>. The unclean person who does not apply them, to be cut off from the congregation, <reference osisRef="Num.19.20">Num 19:20</reference>. This is to be a perpetual statute, <reference osisRef="Num.19.21">Num 19:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.19.22">Num 19:22</reference>.
entries.0e58cd0b252b0ea59be2f20d2f413977642238f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen5741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5742" type="x-p"/> Speak unto the children of Israel that they bring thee, etc. - The ordinance of the red heifer was a sacrifice of general application. All the people were to have an interest in it, and therefore the people at large are to provide the sacrifice. This Jewish rite certainly had a reference to things done under the Gospel, as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews has remarked: "For if," says he, "the blood of bulls and of goats," alluding, probably, to the sin-offerings and the scape-goat, "and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh; how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God!" <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">Heb 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">Heb 9:14</reference>. As the principal stress of the allusion here is to the ordinance of the red heifer, we may certainly conclude that it was designed to typify the sacrifice of our blessed Lord. <div eID="gen5742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5743" type="x-p"/> We may remark several curious particulars in this ordinance. <div eID="gen5743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5744" type="x-p"/> 1. A heifer was appointed for a sacrifice, probably, in opposition to the Egyptian superstition which held these sacred, and actually worshipped their great goddess Isis under this form; and this appears the more likely because males in general were preferred for sacrifice, yet here the female is chosen. <div eID="gen5744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5745" type="x-p"/> 2. It was to be a red heifer, because red bulls were sacrificed to appease the evil demon Typhon, worshipped among the Egyptians. See Spencer. <div eID="gen5745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5746" type="x-p"/> 3. The heifer was to be without spot - having no mixture of any other color. Plutarch remarks, De Iside et de Osiride, that if there was a single hair in the animal either white or black, it marred the sacrifice. See Calmet, and see the note on <reference osisRef="Num.8.7">Num 8:7</reference>. <div eID="gen5746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5747" type="x-p"/> 4. Without blemish - having no kind of imperfection in her body; the other, probably, applying to the hair or color. <div eID="gen5747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5748" type="x-p"/> 5. On which never came yoke, because any animal which had been used for any common purpose was deemed improper to be offered in sacrifice to God. The heathens, who appear to have borrowed much from the Hebrews, were very scrupulous in this particular. Neither the Greeks nor Romans, nor indeed the Egyptians, would offer an animal in sacrifice that had been employed for agricultural purposes. Of this we have the most positive evidence from Homer, Porphyry, Virgil, and Macrobius. <div eID="gen5748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5749" type="x-p"/> Just such a sacrifice as that prescribed here, does Diomede vow to offer to Pallas - Iliad, lib. x., ver. 291. Ὡς νυν μοι εθελουσα παριστασο, και με φυλασσε· Σοι δ' αυ εγω ῥεξω βουν ηνιν ευρυμετωπον, Αδμητην, ἡν ουπω ὑπο ζυγον ηγαγεν ανηρ· Την τοι εγω ῥεξω, χρυσον κερασιν περιχευας. "So now be present, O celestial maid; <div eID="gen5749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5750" type="x-p"/> So still continue to the race thine aid; <div eID="gen5750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5751" type="x-p"/> A yearling heifer falls beneath the stroke, <div eID="gen5751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5752" type="x-p"/> Untamed, unconscious of the galling yoke, <div eID="gen5752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5753" type="x-p"/> With ample forehead and with spreading horns, <div eID="gen5753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5754" type="x-p"/> Whose tapering tops refulgent gold adorns." <div eID="gen5754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5755" type="x-p"/> Altered from Pope. <div eID="gen5755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5756" type="x-p"/> In the very same words Nestor, Odyss., lib. iii., ver. 382, promises a similar sacrifice to Pallas. <div eID="gen5756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5757" type="x-p"/> The Romans had the same religion with the Greeks, and consequently the same kind of sacrifices; so Virgil, Georg. iv., ver. 550. <div eID="gen5757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5758" type="x-p"/> Quatuor eximios praestanti corpore tauros <div eID="gen5758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5759" type="x-p"/> Ducit, et intacta totidem cervice juveneas. " - From his herd he culls <div eID="gen5759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5760" type="x-p"/> For slaughter four the fairest of his bulls; <div eID="gen5760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5761" type="x-p"/> Four heifers from his female stock he took, <div eID="gen5761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5762" type="x-p"/> All fair, and all unknowing of the yoke." <div eID="gen5762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5763" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen5763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5764" type="x-p"/> It is very likely that the Gentiles learnt their first sacrificial rites from the patriarchs; and on this account we need not wonder to find so many coincidences in the sacrificial system of the patriarchs and Jews, and all the neighboring nations.
entries.95d3f6df97b27568afdb78b08f1b426910d56cdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen5764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5765" type="x-p"/> For a water of separation - That is, the ashes were to be kept, in order to be mixed with water, <reference osisRef="Num.19.17">Num 19:17</reference>, and sprinkled on those who had contracted any legal defilement.
entries.cec0d25260e0a6604183ddeda2d1839beb362257: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen5765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5766" type="x-p"/> He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days - How low does this lay man! He who touched a dead beast was only unclean for one day, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.24">Lev 11:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.27">Lev 11:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.39">Lev 11:39</reference>; but he who touches a dead man is unclean for seven days. This was certainly designed to mark the peculiar impurity of man, and to show his sinfulness - seven times worse than the vilest animal! O thou son of the morning, how art thou fallen!
entries.06fa4d7f48a9ebd198ad0e0bc36ea587e39edb08: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen5766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5767" type="x-p"/> He shall purify himself with it - יתחטא בו yithchatta bo, literally, he shall sin himself with it. This Hebrew form of speech is common enough among us in other matters. Thus to fleece, to bark, and to skin, do not signify to add a fleece, another bark, or a skin, but to take one away; therefore, to sin himself, in the Hebrew idiom, is not to add sin, but to take it away, to purify. The verb חטא chata signifies to miss the mark, to sin, to purify from sin, and to make a sin-offering. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.13.13">Gen 13:13</reference>. <div eID="gen5767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5768" type="x-p"/> The Hebrews generally sacrificed males, no matter of what color; but here a heifer, and a heifer of a red color, is ordered. The reason of these circumstances is not very well known. "The rabbins, with all their boldness," says Calmet, "who stick at nothing when it is necessary to explain what they do not understand, declare that the cause of this law is entirely unknown; and that Solomon, with all his wisdom, could not find it out." <div eID="gen5768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5769" type="x-p"/> Several fathers, as well modern as ancient, profess to understand the whole clearly. <div eID="gen5769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5770" type="x-p"/> 1. The red heifer with them signifies the flesh of our Lord, formed out of an earthly substance. <div eID="gen5770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5771" type="x-p"/> 2. Being without spot, etc., the infinite holiness of Christ. <div eID="gen5771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5772" type="x-p"/> 3. The sex of the animal, the infirmity of our flesh, with which he clothed himself. <div eID="gen5772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5773" type="x-p"/> 4. The red color, his passion. <div eID="gen5773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5774" type="x-p"/> 5. Being unyoked, his being righteous in all his conduct, and never under the yoke of sin. <div eID="gen5774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5775" type="x-p"/> 6. Eleazar's sacrificing the heifer instead of Aaron, <reference osisRef="Gen.13.3">Gen 13:3</reference>, signifies the change of the priesthood from the family of Aaron, in order that a new and more perfect priesthood might take place. <div eID="gen5775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5776" type="x-p"/> 7. The red heifer being taken without the camp (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.3">Gen 13:3</reference>) to be slain, points out the crucifixion of our Lord without the city. <div eID="gen5776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5777" type="x-p"/> 8. The complete consuming of the heifer by fire, the complete offering of the whole body and soul of Christ as a sacrifice to God for the sin of man: for as the heifer was without blemish, the whole might be offered to God; and as Christ was immaculate, his whole body and soul were made a sacrifice for sin. <div eID="gen5777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5778" type="x-p"/> 9. As the fire of this sacrifice ascended up to God, so it points out the resurrection and ascension of our blessed Lord. <div eID="gen5778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5779" type="x-p"/> 10. And as the ashes of this victim communicated a legal purity to those who were defiled, so true repentance, signified by those ashes, is necessary for the expiation of the offenses committed after baptism. <div eID="gen5779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5780" type="x-p"/> A great part of this is true in itself; but how little evidence is there that all these things were intended in the ordinance of the red heifer? See on <reference osisRef="Num.8.7">Num 8:7</reference> (note).  <chapter eID="Num.19"/> <div eID="gen5780" type="x-p"/>

entries.2965a90189fd0881428653b8331732582b3da933: Num 19:1 <div eID="gen1837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1838" type="x-p"/> In order that a consciousness of the continuance of the covenant relation might be kept alive during the dying out of the race that had fallen under the judgment of God, after the severe stroke with which the Lord had visited the whole nation in consequence of the rebellion of the company of Korah, He gave the law concerning purification from the uncleanness of death, in which first of all the preparation of a sprinkling water is commanded for the removal of this uncleanness (<hi type="italic">Num 19:1-10</hi>); and then, secondly, the use of this purifying water enjoined as an eternal statute (Num 19:10-22). The thought that death, and the putrefaction of death, as being the embodiment of sin, defiled and excluded from fellowship with the holy God, was a view of the fall and its consequences which had been handed down from the primeval age, and which was not only shared by the Israelites with many of the nations of antiquity,<note placement="foot">Vid., Bähr,<hi type="italic">Symbolik,</hi> ii. pp. 466ff.; <hi type="italic">Sommer, bibl. Abhdll.</hi> pp. 271ff.; <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> on this chapter, and Leyrer in <hi type="italic">Herzog's</hi> Cyclopaedia.</note> but presupposed by the laws given on Sinai as a truth well known in Israel; and at the same time confirmed, both in the prohibition of the priests from defiling themselves with the dead, except in the case of their nearest blood-relations (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.1-Lev.21.6">Lev 21:1-6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.10-Lev.21.12">Lev 21:10-12</reference>), and in the command, that every one who was defiled by a corpse should be removed out of the camp (Num 5:2-4). Now, so long as the mortality within the congregation did not exceed the natural limits, the traditional modes of purification would be quite sufficient. But when it prevailed to a hitherto unheard-of extent, in consequence of the sentence pronounced by God, the defilements would necessarily be so crowded together, that the whole congregation would be in danger of being infected with the defilement of death, and of forfeiting its vocation to be the holy nation of Jehovah, unless God provided it with the means of cleansing itself from this uncleanness, without losing the fellowship of His covenant of grace. The law which follows furnished the means. In Num 19:2 this law is called התּורה חקּת, a “<hi type="italic">statute of instruction,</hi>” or law-statute. This combination of the two words commonly used for law and statute, which is only met with again in Num 31:21, and there, as here, in connection with a rule relating to purification from the uncleanness of death, is probably intended to give emphasis to the design of the law about to be given, to point it out as one of great importance, but not as <hi type="italic">decretum absque ulla ratione</hi>, a decree without any reason, as the Rabbins suppose.
entries.f0b1539dda67d69675d14dfb1db69e6cd81bda58: Num 19:2-10 <div eID="gen1838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1839" type="x-p"/> Preparation of the Purifying Water. - As water is the ordinary means by which all kinds of uncleanness are removed, it was also to be employed in the removal of the uncleanness of death. But as this uncleanness was the strongest of all religious defilements, fresh water alone was not sufficient to remove it; and consequently a certain kind of sprinkling-water was appointed, which was strengthened by the ashes of a sin-offering, and thus formed into a holy alkali. The main point in the law which follows, therefore, was the preparation of the ashes, and these had to be obtained by the <hi type="italic">sacrifice of a red heifer</hi>.<note placement="foot">On this sacrifice, which is so rich in symbolical allusions, but the details of which are so difficult to explain, compare the rabbinical statutes in the talmudical tractate <hi type="italic">Para</hi> (<hi type="italic">Mishnah, v. Surenh.</hi> vi. pp. 269ff.); <hi type="italic">Maimonides de vacca rufa;</hi> and <hi type="italic">Lundius jüd. Heiligth</hi>. pp. 680ff. Among modern treatises on this subject, are <hi type="italic">Bähr’s Symbolik,</hi> ii. pp. 493ff.; Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Egypt and the Books of Moses</hi>, pp. 173ff.; <hi type="italic">Leyrer</hi> in <hi type="italic">Herzog’s Cycl.;</hi> <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Theol. Studien und Kritiken,</hi> 1846, pp. 629ff. (also <hi type="italic">Sacrificial Worship of the Old Testament,</hi> pp. 422ff., Eng. transl., Tr.); and my <hi type="italic">Archäologie</hi>, i. p. 58.</note>  Num 19:2 <div eID="gen1839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1840" type="x-p"/> The sons of Israel were to bring to Moses a red heifer, entirely without blemish, and to give it to Eleazar the priest, that he might have it slaughtered in his presence outside the camp. פּרה is not a cow generally, but a young cow, a heifer, הב́לבכיע (lxx), <hi type="italic">juvenca</hi>, between the calf and the full-grown cow. אדמּה, of a red colour, is not to be connected with תמימה in the sense of “quite red,” as the Rabbins interpret it; but תמימה, <hi type="italic">integra</hi>, is to be taken by itself, and the words which follow, “<hi type="italic">wherein is no blemish,</hi>” to be regarded as defining it still more precisely (see <reference osisRef="Lev.22.19-Lev.22.20">Lev 22:19-20</reference>). The slaying of this heifer is called חטּאת, a sin-offering, in Num 19:9 and Num 19:17. To remind the congregation that death was the wages of sin, the antidote to the defilement of death was to be taken from a sin-offering. But as the object was not to remove and wipe away sin as such, but simply to cleanse the congregation from the uncleanness which proceeded from death, the curse of sin, it was necessary that the sin-offering should be modified in a peculiar manner to accord with this special design. The sacrificial animal was not to be a bullock, as in the case of the ordinary sin-offerings of the congregation (<reference osisRef="Lev.4.14">Lev 4:14</reference>), but a female, because the female sex is the bearer of life (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.20">Gen 3:20</reference>), a פּרה, i.e., lit., the fruit-bringing; and of a red colour, not because the blood-red colour points to sin (as Hengstenberg follows the Rabbins and earlier theologians in supposing), but as the colour of the most “intensive life,” which has its seat in the blood, and shows itself in the red colour of the face (the cheeks and lips); and one “upon which no yoke had ever come,” i.e., whose vital energy had not yet been crippled by labour under the yoke. Lastly, like all the sacrificial animals, it was to be uninjured, and free from faults, inasmuch as the idea of representation, which lay at the foundation of all the sacrifices, but more especially of the sin-offerings, demanded natural sinlessness and original purity, quite as much as imputed sin and transferred uncleanness. Whilst the last-mentioned prerequisite showed that the victim was well fitted for bearing sin, the other attributes indicated the fulness of life and power in their highest forms, and qualified it to form a powerful antidote to death. As thus appointed to furnish a reagent against death and mortal corruption, the sacrificial animal was to possess throughout, viz., in colour, in sex, and in the character of its body, the fulness of life in its greatest freshness and vigour.
entries.55d063c2102b68b795d660531b98232e1fa2864b: Num 19:11-13 <div eID="gen1843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1844" type="x-p"/> Whoever touched a corpse, “<hi type="italic">with regard to all the souls of men,</hi>” i.e., the corpse of a person, of whatever age or sex, was unclean for seven days, and on the third and seventh day he was to cleanse himself (התחטּא, as in Num 8:21) with the water (בּו refers, so far as the sense is concerned, to the water of purification). If he neglected this cleansing, he did not become clean, and he defiled the dwelling of Jehovah (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.15.31">Lev 15:31</reference>). Such a man was to be cut off from Israel (vid., at <reference osisRef="Gen.17.14">Gen 17:14</reference>).
entries.511853dcc3fe1d39cf18631bf25cc6686b9d78c5: Num 19:14-16 <div eID="gen1844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1845" type="x-p"/> Special instructions concerning the defilement. If a man died in a tent, every one who entered it, or who was there at the time, became unclean for seven days. So also did every “<hi type="italic">open vessel upon which there was not a covering, a string,</hi>” i.e., that had not a covering fastened by a string, to prevent the smell of the corpse from penetrating it. פּתיל, a string, is in apposition to צמיד, a band, or binding (see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §113; <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §287, e.). This also applied to any one in the open field, who touched a man who had either been slain by the sword or had died a natural death, or even a bone (skeleton), or a grave.
entries.106ac215c2fa7489b5d9314d328d1986dfbe82d8: Num 19:17-20 <hi type="italic">Ceremony of purification</hi>. They were to take for the unclean person some of the dust of the burning of the cow, i.e., some of the ashes obtained by burning the cow, and put living, i.e., fresh water (see <reference osisRef="Lev.14.5">Lev 14:5</reference>), upon it in a vessel. A clean man was then to take a bunch of hyssop (see <reference osisRef="Exod.12.22">Exo 12:22</reference>), on account of its inherent purifying power, and dip it in the water, on the third and seventh day after the defilement had taken place, and to sprinkle the tent, with the vessels and persons in it, as well as every one who had touched a corpse, whether a person slain, or one who had died a natural death, or a grave; after which the persons were to wash their clothes and bathe, that they might be clean in the evening. As the uncleanness in question is held up as the highest grade of uncleanness, by its duration being fixed at seven days, i.e., an entire week, so the appointment of a double purification with the sprinkling water shows the force of the uncleanness to be removed; whilst the selection of the third and seventh days was simply determined by the significance of the numbers themselves. In Num 19:20, the threat of punishment for the neglect of purification is repeated from Num 19:13, for the purpose of making it most emphatic.
entries.2d2e4a07939420e2d2b2d2477fe989ff64955f67: Num 19:21-22 <div eID="gen1845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1846" type="x-p"/> This also was to be an everlasting statute, that he who sprinkled the water of purification, or even touched it (see at Num 19:7.), and he who was touched by a person defiled (by a corpse), and also the person who touched him, should be unclean till the evening, - a rule which also applied to other forms of uncleanness.  <chapter eID="Num.19"/> <div eID="gen1846" type="x-p"/>

entries.cc6b44d314e43f3448a3a435108d00dfec856987: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.19.2" sID="gen10218" type="section"/> <div sID="gen10219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2</hi> <hi type="italic"> This is the ordinance of the law. </hi>Because it could not but occur that, whilst the faithful were engaged in the world, they should often contract some pollution by their contact with its many impurities, the composition of the water is here described, by the sprinkling of which they might wash away, and expiate their uncleanness: and then certain kinds of pollution are specified, whereof the purification is required. God commands that a red heifer should be slain, which had never been subjected to the yoke; and that it should be burnt without the camp, together with its skin and dung; that the ashes should be gathered by a man that was clean, and laid up without the camp for the common use of the people. But, in order that the water, which was mixed with these ashes, should have the power of reconciliation, God at the same time commands that the blood should be sprinkled seven times before the altar by the finger of the priest. The object of this ceremony was twofold: for God would awaken the attention of the people to reflect more closely upon their impurity; and, although they might be pure within, still would have them carefully look around them, lest they should be polluted from without; and also taught them that, as often as they were infected by any pollution, expiation was to be sought for from elsewhere, viz., from sacrifice and sprinkling; and thus admonish them that men inquire in vain in themselves for the remedies demanded for their purification, because purity can only proceed from the sanctuary. Those, who speculate subtilty on the details, advance some questionable matters. I leave them, therefore, to the enjoyment of their conceits; let it suffice for us to consider generally what God referred to in this ceremony, and what advantage accrued from it to the people. By the red color, they suppose that sin is signified. Meanwhile, lest they should run into a manifest contradiction, they are obliged absurdly to interpret what follows, that He required a heifer perfect and without blemish, as if it were said that there should be no difference of color in her hair; whereas God demands the same thing as in the other sacrifices, which were rejected as faulty if any mark of deformity existed in them. And in this sense it is added that she should never have borne a yoke. Therefore I make no doubt but that God enjoined that a pure heifer, neither mutilated nor lame, should be chosen; and, that her perfectness might be more apparent, as yet unbroken to the yoke. What, then, is the meaning of the red color? First of all, I prefer confessing my ignorance to advancing anything doubtful; but it may be conjectured that a common and ordinary color was rather chosen, lest it should be too conspicuous, as it would have been, if either white or black. But this should be deemed sure, that a perfect heifer, and one free from every blemish, was to be offered, and one too, which had not been broken to bear the yoke by the hands of men, that the purification might have nothing of humanity about it.: But the command to offer her was given to the whole people; because, in order that we may be partakers of ablution, it is necessary that each of us should offer Christ to the Father. For, although He only, and that but once, has offered Himself, still a daily offering of Him, which is effected by faith and prayers, is enjoined to us, not such as <note n="22"> <div sID="gen10220" type="x-p"/> See the dogmatical statement of this notion in the Creed of Pius iv.<div eID="gen10220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10221" type="x-p"/>Art: V. — “I profess, likewise, that in the Mass there is offered to God a true, proper, and propitiatory sacrifice for the living and the dead; and that in the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist there are truly, really, and substantially the body and blood, together with the soul and divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.<div eID="gen10221" type="x-p"/> </note> the Papists have invented, by whom in their impiety and perverseness, the Lord’s Supper has been mistakenly turned into a sacrifice, because they imagined that Christ must be daily slain, in order that His death might profit us. The offering, however, of faith and prayers, of which I speak, is very different, and by it alone we apply to ourselves the virtue and fruit of Christ’s death.<div eID="gen10219" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen10218" osisID="Num.19.2" type="section"/>
entries.556ab770fcde5c3d44aea9790f2156919ec49918: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.19.3" sID="gen10222" type="section"/> <div sID="gen10223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3</hi> <hi type="italic">And ye shall give her unto Eleazar. </hi>A clear distinction is here made between two offerings; for the people are not permitted to kill the heifer, but this is the peculiar office of the priest. Thus the people offered vicariously by the hand of the priest; and in this way also at present, although we set Christ before God’s face in order to propitiate Him, still it is necessary that Christ Himself should interpose, and exercise the office of a priest. Again, the heifer was to be taken outside the camp, as a sign that it was accursed, since it was an atonement. On which account, too, the atoning victims, whose blood was carried into the Holy of Holies, were burnt without the camp; the truth of which figure was accomplished in Christ, who therefore suffered outside the gates of the city, as the Apostle testifies. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.11-Heb.13.12">Hebrews 13:11-12</reference>.) But, because this was a species of rejection, lest the heifer should be less accounted of, or lest the Israelites should think her polluted by the curse, God shews that her blood was sacred and of a sweet savor, by commanding that it should be sprinkled seven times upon the altar, which might not be profaned by anything unclean. The same thing is most clearly seen in Christ; for although He was made a curse for us, and is called “sin<hi type="italic">,</hi>” because by bearing our accursed sins upon the cross, He was our atoning victim, yet nothing was thereby taken from His purity, so as to prevent His holiness from being the sanctification of the whole world. For He offered Himself through the Spirit, and by His own blood entered into the holy place, and His death is elsewhere called by Paul, “a sacrifice for a sweet-smelling savor.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.11-Heb.9.12">Hebrews 9:11-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.2">Ephesians 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.4.18">Philippians 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen10223" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen10222" osisID="Num.19.3" type="section"/>
entries.2aecc487a5971717cf4c1a7f23f13cd29a19bef2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.19.6" sID="gen10224" type="section"/> <div sID="gen10225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6</hi> <hi type="italic">And the priest shall take cedar-wood. </hi>That the sprinkling of the blood might be conjoined with that of the water, the cedar-wood, and hyssop, and scarlet, thread, with which the sprinkling was wont to be made, were cast into the fire; for, unless the Israelites had been admonished by this visible sign, they would not have so clearly known that they were not only washed with the water, but that by the offering of the sacrifice also their uncleanness was removed. But it was not enough that the blood should be poured forth, unless, as has been already seen, they were purified by its aspersion. But, for as much as the scent of cedar-wood is precious, and in hyssop there is a cleansing property, we gather from hence also that the victim was pure, although it bore their sins together with the curse and expiation. Peter teaches us how we are sprinkled with the blood of Christ, viz., through the Spirit, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.2">1 Peter 1:2</reference>;) nay, John shews us in his Canonical Epistle, that we find all the parts of this ceremony in Christ, where he writes that Christ “came by water and blood,” and “it is the Spirit that beareth witness, because the Spirit is truth.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.5.6">1 John 5:6</reference>.)<div eID="gen10225" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen10224" osisID="Num.19.6" type="section"/>
entries.b2b5e96c5255a4b02b8920830278fa94b9f72fa5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.19.7" sID="gen10226" type="section"/> <div sID="gen10227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7</hi> <hi type="italic">Then the priest shall wash his clothes. </hi>At first sight there seems to be a discrepancy in the facts, that the heifer was sacred to God, and pure, and still that the priest was polluted by touching it; yet they accord very well with each other. But that both the priest as well as the minister who made the burning, were unclean until the evening, ought to have forcibly struck the people, and taught them the more to abominate sin. And, since it was not permitted to any but a man that was clean to gather the ashes, not that they should be laid anywhere but in a clean place, it was manifested by this sign that there was no impurity in the sacrifice itself, but that from an extraneous and adventitious pollution; because it was destined to purge away uncleanness, it was accounted in a certain sense unclean. Whence too the water, into which the ashes were thrown, was called the water of separation, as well as the expiation <note n="23"> <div sID="gen10228" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Nam expiatio est</foreign>.” — <hi type="italic">Lat</hi>, v. 9. “It is a purification for sin.” — <hi type="italic">A.V</hi>.<div eID="gen10228" type="x-p"/> </note> For this translation which I have given is the right one; and others improperly render it “for waters of separation, and for expiation.” The old interpreter has not given the sense amiss, as far as regards this word, “<hi type="italic">because </hi>the heifer is burnt for sin.” But since in Hebrew the word,<foreign xml:lang="he">חטאה </foreign> <hi type="italic">chateah</hi> <note n="24"> <div sID="gen10229" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="he">למי נדה חטאת הוא</foreign> <foreign xml:lang="el">́̔Υδωρ ῥαντισμᾶ ἅγνισμά ἐστι·</foreign> — <hi type="italic">LXX. </hi><foreign xml:lang="la">In aqua aspersionis; quia pro peccato vacca combusta est</foreign>. — V. This last is what <hi type="italic">C</hi>. means by “the old interpreter.” The translation which he condemns he had seen in <hi type="italic">S.M</hi>. — W.<div eID="gen10229" type="x-p"/> </note> means not only wickedness or sin, but also the sacrifice on which the curse is imposed; what Moses intended to convey is better expressed by the word “<hi type="italic">expiation.</hi>” But the expression “separation” has reference to the men, whose personal uncleanness excluded them from the holy congregation. But the question arises, why this ordinance is pronounced to be common to the strangers who sojourned in the land of Israel, as well as to the natives; because it was by no means reasonable that the uncircumcised should be purified. The reply is easy, that such strangers are not adverted to as were altogether aliens from the people, but those who, although born of heathen parentage, had embraced the Law. These God equalizes with the children of Abraham in the sacrifices and other religious services; for if their condition were different, the-church, into the body of which they were ingrafted, would be rent asunder.<div eID="gen10227" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen10226" osisID="Num.19.7" type="section"/>
entries.e09ee0d2dc88dfbccfc547a2ca3d3da0b981f223: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.19.11" sID="gen10230" type="section"/> <div sID="gen10231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11. </hi><hi type="italic">He that toucheth the dead body. </hi>He now recites certain forms of pollution in which the washing was necessary; all of them, however, come to the point, that men are defiled by the touch of a corpse or, bones, or a grave. Nor is there here any distinction between the body of a person who is slain, or of one who has died in bed; whence it follows that death is here set forth as a mirror of God’s curse: And assuredly, if we consider its origin and cause, the corruption of nature, whereby the image of God is defaced, presents itself in every, dead man; for, unless we were altogether corrupt, we should not be born to perish But God also taught His people by another mode of signifying it, that uncleanness is contracted by our communication with the unfruitful works of darkness. For the Apostle (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.1">Hebrews 6:1</reference>) calls them “dead works,” either from their consequences, or because, as faith is the life of the soul, so unbelief keeps it in death. Since, then, the corpse the bones, the grave, designate whatever we bring from the womb, because, until we are born again, and God quickens us by His Spirit and faith, we are dead while we live; there is no question but that the children of Israel were reminded, that in order to keep themselves pure before God, they must abstain from all corruption; inasmuch as, if they were rendered unclean by their contact with a dead man, they must immediately have recourse to ablution. In fine, the ceremony had no other object than that they should serve God in pureness from the sins of the flesh; and exercise themselves in constant thoughts of repentance, whilst, if they fell from their purity, they should labor to obtain reconciliation with God, by means of sacrifice and ablution.<div eID="gen10231" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen10230" osisID="Num.19.11" type="section"/>
entries.020b224e3321eab4c6275280adaceffd5c332248: <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Num.19.13" sID="gen10232" type="section"/> <div sID="gen10233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">Whosoever toucheth the dead body.</hi> The severity of. the capital punishment shews how very pleasing to God is purity. If any one bad forgotten to sprinkle himself on the third or the seventh day, he might redeem his negligence by a prolongation of the term, because he only postponed his purification to another day; but it was a capital crime to enter the sanctuary in his uncleanness, since thus holy and profane things would be mixed together, nay, the altar would have been polluted as well as the whole service of God. But indeed the act of touching a dead body was of slight importance, nor was it to be deemed an atrocious crime; but here the external defilement is not regarded in itself, as if God were wroth on account of a stain contracted by the performance of a pious duty. <note n="25"> <div sID="gen10234" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour ensevelir son pere</foreign>;” by burying his father — <hi type="italic">Fr.</hi><div eID="gen10234" type="x-p"/> </note> Rather must the object of the <hi type="italic">ceremony </hi>be considered, for God designed by these rudiments to teach the Israelites, like children, that if any one should pollute sacred things by his impurity, he would by no means be tolerated in this audacity. In this then consisted the religious import of the transaction, that the worship of God was too precious for the Israelites to be permitted to contaminate it with impunity. Whence we gather that the punishment was denounced as against sacrilege. In sum, it comes to this, that God is not duly worshipped except with a sincere heart and pure hands; and that if any pollution be contracted<hi type="italic">, </hi>there is need of expiation before a free access is re-opened to holy things. But it must be remarked as to the contact, that it was accounted the same thing, whether the corpse lay in a field or a house; whilst, if any one died in a tent, men were polluted by merely entering it, and likewise vessels without covers thus became unclean.<div eID="gen10233" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Num.19.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen10232" osisID="Num.19.13" type="section"/>

                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And he that gathereth the ashes of the hei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fer, shall wash his clothes, and be unclean untill the even: and it shall be unto the children of Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael, and unto the stranger that sojourneth among them <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To wit, a Proselyte, not any stranger, as some understand it.                   <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 21. 1. chap. 5. 2. Lam. 4. 14. Hag. 2. 13.</ns0:note> He that toucheth the dead body of any <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> soul.</ns0:note> man, shall be unclean seven dayes <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Whereas the touch of a dead beast made a man unclean onely till even, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 11. 24.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 31. 19.</ns0:note> He shall purifie himself with it <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) With the water of separation.</ns0:note> on the third day <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To Typifie Christs resurrection on that day, by which we are cleansed or sancti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied.</ns0:note>, and on the seventh day he shall be clean <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To teach us, that our purification in this life is gra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dual, and not perfect till we come to that eternal Sabbath which the seventh day respected.</ns0:note>: but if he purifie not himself the third day, then the seventh day he shall not be clean <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">But was first to purifie himself and four dayes after that to be clean.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Whosoever toucheth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To wit, if this transgression be done presumptuously, for if it was done ignorantly, he was onely to offer sacrifice, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 5. 3, 6, 17.</ns0:note> the dead body of any man that is dead, and purifieth not himself <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To wit, if this transgression be done presumptuously, for if it was done ignorantly, he was onely to offer sacrifice, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 5. 3, 6, 17.</ns0:note>, defileth the tabernacle of the LORD <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">By approaching to it in his uncleanness: for Holy things or places were ceremonially defiled with the touch of any unclean person or thing.                   <ns0:p n="14">14 This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the law, when a man dieth in a tent, all that come into the tent, and all that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the tent, shall be unclean seven days.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And every <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 31. 20.</ns0:note> open vessel <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Because it receives the air of the tent, by which it is cere<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monially polluted.                   <ns0:p n="16">16 And whosoever toucheth one that is slain with a sword <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or by any other violent way.</ns0:note> in the open fields, or a dead bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy, or a bone of a man, or a grave, shall be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clean seven dayes.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And the clean <ns0:hi>person</ns0:hi> shall sprinkle upon the unclean on the third day, and on the seventh day: and on the seventh day, he shall purifie him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, and wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and shall be clean at even.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 But the man that shall be unclean, and shall not purifie himself <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Shall contemptuously refuse to submit to this way of purification.</ns0:note>, that soul shall be cut off from among the congregation: because he hath defiled the sanctuary of the LORD, the water of separation hath not been sprinkled upon him, he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unclean.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And it shall be a perpetual statute unto them that he that sprinkleth the water of separa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion shall wash his clothes <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Because he is unclean, as it here follows. It is strange, that the same water should cleanse one person, and defile ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, but God would have it so, partly to teach us that it did not cleanse by any vertue in it or in the work done, but onely by vertue of Gods appointment: partly to mind the Jews of the imperfection of their Priesthood and their ritual purificati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons and expiations, and consequently of the necessity of a bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter Priest and sacrifice and way of purifying, which these out<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward Rites did point at: and partly to shew that the efficacy of Gods ordinances doth not depend upon the person or qua<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lity of his Ministers, because the same person who was pollu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted himself could and did cleanse others.</ns0:note>: and he that touch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the water of separation <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either by sprink<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling of it, or by being sprinkled with it, for even he that was cleansed by it, was not fully cleansed as soon as he was sprink<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led, but onely at the even of that day, as is said here and a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note>, shall be unclean until even.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And whatsoever the unclean <ns0:hi>person</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not he who is so onely by touching the water of separati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 21. but he who is so by the greater sort of uncleanness, which lasted seven days, of which <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 11, 16. and which was not removed without the use of this water of purification, as is manifest from the context and other places of Scripture, and from the nature of the thing: For the lesser sort of unclean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, mentioned in the foregoing verse, lasted onely till even, and was cleansed by the sole washing of his clothes and flesh in water, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 7. without any use of this water of purification, which, if it had been necessary, must have been used on the third, and on the seventh day, according to the rule, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 12, 19. and so the uncleanness of one day had been made an un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cleanness of seven days, which is a contradiction. Besides it is unreasonable, that he who immediately touched the defiling thing should be no more and longer unclean, than he who touched that person onely; and it is contrary to other rules in like cases, as <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 15. where the Man or Woman having an issue are thereby made unclean for seven days, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 13, 28. but he who toucheth them is made unclean onely till even, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 7, 27. And therefore this cannot be meant of him who was unclean by touching this water, who himself was unclean onely till even, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 21. as also he who toucheth him is in this place.</ns0:note> touch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth, shall be unclean: and the soul that toucheth <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> shall be unclean <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To signifie to us, the very infectious nature of sin and of sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />full company.</ns0:note> until even <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Because as his defilement was less, so it was fit the duration of it should be shorter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
